plain_english: Now let's talk about money and possessions — the biggest source of human misery. Compare all our other troubles — death, illness, fear, regret, physical pain and hard work — with the suffering that money causes us. Money troubles will always be worse. Think about this: it hurts much less to never have had money than to lose it. This shows us that the less you have, the less you can lose, and the less you'll suffer. Poor people don't feel financial losses any less than rich people do. You're wrong if you think wealthy people handle losses better. A wound hurts the same whether you're big or small.
original_excerpt: Let us now pass on to the consideration of property, that most fertile source of human sorrows: for if you compare all the other ills from which we suffer—deaths, sicknesses, fears, regrets, endurance of pains and labours— with those miseries which our money inflicts upon us, the latter will far outweigh all the others. Reflect, then, how much less a grief it is never to have had any money than to have lost it: we shall thus understand that the less poverty has to lose, the less torment it has with which to afflict us: for you are mistaken if you suppose that the rich bear their losses with greater spirit than the poor: a wound causes the same amount of pain to the greatest and the smallest body.

plain_english: Bion had a clever saying: "Pulling out hair hurts just as much whether you're bald or have a full head of hair." You can be sure the same is true for rich and poor people — they suffer equally when they lose money. Money sticks to both types of people and can't be torn away without pain. But as I've said, it's easier to bear not getting something in the first place than losing what you already have. That's why you'll find that people who never had good luck are happier than people who had it and lost it.
original_excerpt: It was a neat saying of Bion's, "that it hurts bald men as much as hairy men to have their hairs pulled out": you may be assured that the same thing is true of rich and poor people, that their suffering is equal: for their money clings to both classes, and cannot be torn away without their feeling it: yet it is more endurable, as I have said, and easier not to gain property than to lose it, and therefore you will find that those upon whom Fortune has never smiled are more cheerful than those whom she has deserted.

plain_english: Diogenes, a man with enormous spirit, understood this truth. He made it impossible for anyone to take anything away from him. You can call this freedom from loss by any name you want — poverty, want, necessity, or whatever insulting term you prefer. I still think such a man is happy, unless you can show me another person who has nothing to lose. If I'm right, it's a kingly quality in a world full of greedy people, cheaters, and thieves to be the one man who cannot be harmed. Anyone who doubts that Diogenes was happy might as well doubt whether the immortal gods are happy enough — since they don't own farms or gardens, don't have valuable estates rented out to tenants, and don't make big loans in the financial markets.
original_excerpt: Diogenes, a man of infinite spirit, perceived this, and made it impossible that anything should be taken from him. Call this security from loss poverty, want, necessity, or any contemptuous name you please: I shall consider such a man to be happy, unless you find me another who can lose nothing. If I am not mistaken, it is a royal attribute among so many misers, sharpers, and robbers, to be the one man who cannot be injured. If any one doubts the happiness of Diogenes, he would doubt whether the position of the immortal gods was one of sufficient happiness. because they have no farms or gardens, no valuable estates let to strange tenants, and no large loans in the money market.

plain_english: Aren't you embarrassed? You stare at wealth with wide-eyed wonder. Look at the universe instead. The gods own nothing, yet they give us everything. Do you think a person who has stripped away all these random possessions is poor? Or do you think he's more like the immortal gods? Would you call Demetrius — Pompey's former slave — a happier man? He wasn't ashamed to be richer than his old master. Every day someone brought him a list counting his slaves, like a general getting reports on his army. But he deserved nothing more than two assistants and a prison cell slightly bigger than the other slaves got.
original_excerpt: Are you not ashamed of yourself, you who gaze upon riches with astonished admiration? Look upon the universe: you will see the gods quite bare of property, and possessing nothing though they give everything. Do you think that this man who has stripped himself of all fortuitous accessories is a pauper, or one like to the immortal gods? Do you call Demetrius, Pompeius's freedman, a happier man, he who was not ashamed to be richer than Pompeius, who was daily furnished with a list of the number of his slaves, as a general is with that of his army, though he had long deserved that all his riches should consist of a pair of underlings, and a roomier cell than the other slaves?

plain_english: But Diogenes had only one slave, and that slave ran away from him. When someone pointed out where the slave was, Diogenes didn't think he was worth bringing back. "It would be shameful," he said, "if Manes can live without Diogenes, but Diogenes can't live without Manes." To me, it sounds like he was saying, "Fortune, mind your own business! Diogenes has nothing left that you can take from me. Did my slave run away? No — he left me as a free man."
original_excerpt: But Diogenes's only slave ran away from him, and when he was pointed out to Diogenes, he did not think him worth fetching back. "It is a shame," he said, "that Manes should be able to live without Diogenes, and that Diogenes should not be able to live without Manes." He seems to me to have said, "Fortune, mind your own business: Diogenes has nothing left that belongs to you. Did my slave run away? nay, he went away from me as a free man."

plain_english: A household full of slaves needs food and clothes. You have to feed all those hungry mouths. You have to buy them clothing and watch their sticky fingers. And you have to rely on people who hate you and curse your name. How much happier is the person who owes nothing to anyone — except for things he can easily give up! But since we don't have that kind of mental strength, we should at least reduce what we own. This makes us less vulnerable to fortune's attacks. In war, soldiers who can fit inside their armor fight better than those whose huge size sticks out everywhere, exposing them to wounds. The best amount of wealth is just enough to keep you out of poverty — but not much more than that.
original_excerpt: A household of slaves requires food and clothing: the bellies of so many hungry creatures have to be filled: we must buy raiment for them, we must watch their most thievish hands, and we must make use of the services of people who weep and execrate us. How far happier is he who is indebted to no man for anything except for what he can deprive himself of with the greatest ease! Since we, however, have not such strength of mind as this, we ought at any rate to diminish the extent of our property, in order to be less exposed to the assaults of fortune: those men whose bodies can be within the shelter of their armour, are more fitted for war than those whose huge size everywhere extends beyond it, and exposes them to wounds: the best amount of property to have is that which is enough to keep us from poverty, and which yet is not far removed from it.
